voiceover: Relatives asking about your wedding? Use these replies. Copy, Paste, Send. Today's awkward message: the question at the holiday table. I'm Norah, Wedillybird's AI host. Six questions, six replies. First, agree your answers with your partner. Rehearse them once, then answer as a team. Question one: When is it, and are we invited? Say: We're finalizing the list and will reach out personally once it's set. It's honest, it's kind, and it promises nothing. Question two: Where do we stay? Say: We'll share hotel and travel details with the invitation. Holiday weekend date? Tell relatives early, because calendars fill up. Here's the part people skip: you can be warm and still hold the line. Question three: You should really do it this way. Say: Thank you for the suggestion. We'll keep it in mind. You don't have to use the idea. You can still thank them. Follow if a winter wedding is ahead. Tomorrow: five things people forget. Question four: We could host it at our place. Say: We've chosen the venue. We'd love for you to host the rehearsal dinner. State your position first, then offer a compromise. Question five: We'd like to help pay. Accept graciously, because refusing can do more harm than good. Say: Thank you, that's generous. We'd love your input, and we'll finalize details ourselves. Question six: In our family, we always do it this way. Say: We'd love to find a small way to honor that during the ceremony. Notice what every reply does. Thank them, state your position, offer a compromise. The pinned comment has all six, word for word. Save this for the first holiday dinner. Relatives asking about your wedding? caption:
What to say when relatives ask about your wedding: six word-for-word replies for the holiday table, from "are we invited?" to "we'd like to help pay".
Hosted by Norah, an AI character created by the Wedillybird team.
pinned_comment:
Six replies for the holiday table (swap in your own details):
1. "When is it, and are we invited?" Reply: "We're finalizing the list and will reach out personally once it's set."
2. "Where do we stay?" Reply: "We'll share hotel and travel details with the invitation." (Holiday-weekend date? Tell relatives early.)
3. "You should really do it this way." Reply: "Thank you for the suggestion. We'll keep it in mind."
4. "We could host it at our place." Reply: "We've chosen [venue]. We'd love for you to host the rehearsal dinner."
5. "We'd like to help pay." Reply: "Thank you, that's generous. We'd love your input, and we'll finalize the details ourselves."
6. "In our family, we always do it this way." Reply: "We'd love to find a small way to honor that during the ceremony."
Every reply: thank them, state your position, offer a compromise. Agree your answers with your partner first.
Wording is suggested, built on positions from Zola and Emily Post; it is not a quote.
Norah is AI-generated.
comment_bait: Which question did a relative already ask you?

sources.fact: Advice overload: thank them, keep what helps, let go of the rest; location or hosting demands: make your position clear, then offer a compromise such as hosting the rehearsal dinner; a firm answer is not rude, both Zola and Emily Post advise holding the line politely
sources.title: Who Has a Say in the Wedding Guest List?

sources.fact: Positions behind the suggested scripts (set boundaries, compromise on hosting)
sources.title: Just Engaged?

sources.fact: Talk openly with your partner first and present a united front; accept money graciously because rejecting it may cause more harm than good; compromise on traditions, perhaps including smaller ones in the ceremony; respect opinions without having to use them; on hosting demands state your position and offer a compromise
sources.title: How to Manage Your In-Laws' Expectations for Your Wedding

sources.fact: Contributors get input, not control: this is not their party, it is still yours
sources.title: Who Has a Say in the Wedding Guest List?

sources.fact: Holiday weekends bring more date conflicts and crowded travel; Zola advises earlier save-the-dates for holiday-weekend weddings
sources.title: When to Send Out Wedding Invitations

sources.fact: Include local hotel and transportation information in the invitations because winter weather can disrupt travel
sources.title: Before You Book: Things to Consider When Planning a Winter Wedding

claims_review.notes: No statistics. The scripts are suggested wording built on published positions (T75 is explicit that its five lines are not quotes); replies one (the list question) and two (travel) are original suggested wording, reply two following Mindy Weiss's hotel and transport advice (T62, medium). 'It's honest, it's kind, and it promises nothing' is editorial. The Zola save-the-date window for holiday weekends (ten to twelve months) is deliberately left to D15 so the number is not repeated. T26's 'input, not control' is used once, briefly, because D10 covers it in depth. No product shown or described; the only brand mention is the AI-host disclosure.
